We will show that if there are n pairs (so 2n socks) and one draws socks one‐by‐one (without replacement) until a matching pair is obtained, then if T is the (random) number of socks drawn the answer can be written in “closed‐form” as

  E[T] = (2^(2n)·(n!)²)/( (2n)! ).

In our problem n = 2024 so that the expected total number of socks drawn is

  E[T] = (2^(4048)·(2024!)²)/(4048!).

Since the very last sock drawn completes a pair, the number of “unpaired” socks (that is, those socks that do not have their mate among those drawn) is T – 2. (Every time you stop you have exactly one complete pair and all the others are “lonely”.) Thus one acceptable answer is

  Expected number of unpaired socks = (2^(4048)·(2024!)²)/(4048!) – 2.

Below we describe one way to arrive at this answer.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
A way to derive the answer

Suppose you have n pairs (so 2n socks). Label the pairs 1,2,…,n. You draw socks uniformly at random (without replacement) until you get a pair. (It is clear that you must draw at least 2 socks.) One may show that if
  P(no pair in the first k draws) = A(k)
then
  A(1)=1 and A(k)=∏₍ᵢ₌₁₎^(k–1) [(2n – 2i)/(2n – i)] for k ≥ 2.
Then the probability that the first matching pair occurs on the kth draw is
  P(T=k) = A(k–1) – A(k)  (for k ≥ 2),
and by the “tail‐sum formula” one may show that
  E[T] = Σ₍ⱼ₌₀₎^(2n–1) A(j).
A (not‐so‐obvious) calculation shows that in fact
  E[T] = (2^(2n)·(n!)²)/( (2n)! ).
A quick check in the small cases is reassuring. For example, if n = 2 (so 4 socks) one may verify that
  E[T] = (2⁴·(2!)²)/(4!) = (16·4)/24 = 64/24 = 8/3,
so that the expected number of unpaired socks is 8/3 – 2 = 2/3.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Thus, for n = 2024 the answer is

  (2^(4048)·(2024!)²)/(4048!) – 2.

Any answer equivalent to the expression above is correct.

We will show that one acceptable answer is

  Expected unpaired socks = 
    Σₖ₌₂^(2024) [ (C(2024, k)·2ᵏ)⁄C(4048, k) ].

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at an answer equivalent to the answer above.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
The Problem Setup

Rishabh has 2024 pairs of socks (that is, 4048 socks in all). He draws socks one‐by‐one uniformly at random (without replacement) until he gets a “match” (that is, until he draws a sock which is the mate of one he has already drawn). When he stops the drawn collection consists of one “completed pair” (two socks that match) and some number of “unpaired” socks (each coming from a different pair). (For example, if he stops after drawing 3 socks then one pair is completed and one sock is “unpaired”.) Our goal is to compute the expected number of unpaired socks at the moment he stops.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
A Way to Think About the Process

Notice that if we let T be the (random) draw on which a pair is completed then the drawn set consists of T socks, two of which form a pair and the remaining T–2 are “unpaired.” Hence the number of unpaired socks is T–2 and our desired answer is E[T]–2.

A standard method for problems of this type is to “stop when a repeat occurs.” (This is analogous to the “birthday‐problem”.) In our situation the key observation is that when drawing socks one‐by‐one, as long as no pair has appeared the socks drawn must all come from different pairs. (In other words, if you have drawn r socks and no pair has yet appeared then these r socks come from r different pairs.)

Thus, if we define, for 1 ≤ r ≤ 2024, the event

  Aᵣ = “the first r socks are all from different pairs,”

then the probability of Aᵣ is

  P(Aᵣ) = (number of ways to choose r socks with no pair)⁄(number of ways to choose r socks)
       = [C(2024, r)·2ʳ]⁄C(4048, r).

Now, note that if the first r socks are all from different pairs then the (r+1)–st sock will complete a pair with probability
  r⁄(4048–r)
(because among the 4048–r socks remaining exactly r are the mates of the r already–drawn socks). In other words, the chance that the very first time a pair is completed is on draw r+1 is

  P(T = r+1) = P(Aᵣ)·[r⁄(4048–r)].

Then one may show (by a standard “tail–sum” argument) that
  E[T] = 1 + Σᵣ₌₁^(2024) P(Aᵣ).
Since the number of unpaired socks is T–2, we have

  E[# unpaired] = E[T] – 2 = (Σᵣ₌₁^(2024) P(Aᵣ)) – 1.

But observe that P(A₁)=1 (since the first sock is “unpaired” by definition) so that

  E[# unpaired] = Σᵣ₌₂^(2024) P(Aᵣ)
          = Σᵣ₌₂^(2024) [C(2024, r)·2ʳ⁄C(4048, r)].

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Thus one acceptable answer is

  Expected number of unpaired socks = Σₖ₌₂^(2024) [ (C(2024, k)·2ᵏ)⁄C(4048, k) ].

Any answer equivalent to the answer above is correct.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
A Few Comments

• There is nothing “magical” about the answer – it is obtained by writing the probability that the first r socks are all from different pairs and then using a standard formula for the expectation of a nonnegative, integer–valued random variable (namely, E[T] = 1 + Σₖ₌₁^(∞) P(T > k)).

• (One may check on small examples. For instance, if there is just 1 pair then one always gets T = 2 and so the expected number of unpaired socks is 0. For 2 pairs one may show that the answer is 2⁄3.)

• (There are other ways to write the answer. For example, one might show that
  E[T] = 1 + Σᵣ₌₁^(2024) [C(2024, r)·2ʳ⁄C(4048, r)]
so that the answer is also
  E[# unpaired] = Σᵣ₌₁^(2024) [C(2024, r)·2ʳ⁄C(4048, r)] – 1.)

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Final Answer

An acceptable answer to the problem is

  Σₖ₌₂^(2024) [ (C(2024, k)·2ᵏ)⁄C(4048, k) ].

Any answer equivalent to the answer above is correct.

We will show that the answer can be written in “closed‐form”. (Any answer equivalent to the answer below is correct.)

Suppose Rishabh has 2024 pairs of socks (so 4048 socks in all). He draws socks one‐by‐one (without replacement) until he gets a “match” – that is, until for the first time he draws a sock that is the mate of one he already has. (In particular, note that if the very first two socks match, then he stops with two socks – and in that case there are no “unpaired” socks, since the pair is complete.) In general, if he stops at the Tth draw then the first T–1 socks are all from different pairs and the Tth sock “completes” one of those pairs. (Thus the number of “unpaired” socks he has is T–2.)

A very nice way to “solve” the problem is to show that if we call N the number of pairs (here N = 2024) then one may prove that

  Expected number of unpaired socks = 
    Σ₍ₘ₌₁₎^(N) [2ᵐ · (N choose m)]⁄( (2N choose m) ) – 1.

(To explain briefly: One may show that the probability that the first k draws are all “distinct” (that is, no pair has yet been completed) is
  P(T > k) = [2^(k–1) · (N choose k–1)]⁄( (2N choose k–1) ),
so that by a standard “tail‐sum” formula
  E[T] = Σ₍ₖ₌₁₎^(2N) P(T > k)
and hence
  E[T – 2] = Σ₍ₘ₌₁₎^(N) [2ᵐ · (N choose m)]⁄( (2N choose m) ) – 1.
A short check in the small cases N = 1, 2, 3 shows that this formula is correct.)

Thus, with N = 2024 the answer is

  Expected number of unpaired socks = 
    [ Σ₍ₘ₌₁₎^(2024) (2ᵐ · (2024 choose m))/( (4048 choose m) ) ] – 1.

Any answer equivalent to the answer above is correct.

For example, one acceptable answer was:

  (2¹·C(2024,1)/C(4048,1) + 2²·C(2024,2)/C(4048,2) + … + 2^(2024)·C(2024,2024)/C(4048,2024)) – 1.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
A Note on “How to arrive at this answer”: 

One may think of the process as “drawing a random permutation” of the 4048 socks. Then the process stops at the first time a sock appears whose mate appears earlier. (In other words, if for each pair the two socks appear in some order, the stopping time is the minimum over all pairs of the later‐occurring sock.) A short calculation shows that the probability the first k draws are all from different pairs is
  P(T > k) = [2^(k–1)·(N choose k–1)]⁄( (2N choose k–1) ).
Then by writing
  E[T] = Σ₍ₖ₌₁₎^(∞) P(T > k)
and noting that T – 2 is exactly the number of “unpaired” socks at the moment he stops, one may show that
  E[T – 2] = Σ₍ₘ₌₁₎^(N) [2ᵐ·(N choose m)]⁄( (2N choose m) ) – 1.
(One may check that when N = 2 or 3 the answer comes out correctly.)

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Final answer (with N = 2024):

  Expected number of unpaired socks = 
    [ Σ₍ₘ₌₁₎^(2024) (2ᵐ · C(2024, m))/( C(4048, m) ) ] – 1.

Any answer equivalent to the answer above is correct.

We will show that one acceptable answer is

  Expected unpaired socks = 
    Σ₍ⱼ₌₁₎^(2024) [C(2024, j)·2^j]⁄C(4048, j).

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at an answer equivalent to the answer above.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
A little background

Suppose you have 2024 pairs of socks (so 4048 socks in all) and you draw them one‐by‐one uniformly at random without replacement. You stop as soon as you draw a sock that “matches” (i.e. is the mate of) one you have already drawn. (Note that the very first sock you draw is “unpaired” by definition.) If T is the (random) draw on which you get your first matching pair, then the number of socks that are still “unpaired” when you stop is T – 1. (For example, if you stop on the 3rd draw then you have 2 unpaired socks and the 3rd sock “completes” a pair.)

A standard way to attack such problems is to “mark” the event that the first k socks you draw all come from different pairs. (In other words, no sock drawn in positions 1,…,k is the mate of a sock already drawn.) Then one may show that

  P(the first k socks are all from different pairs)
    = [C(2024, k)·2^k]⁄C(4048, k).

Why? To choose k socks that all come from different pairs you may first choose k pairs out of 2024 (in C(2024,k) ways) and then, from each chosen pair, choose one of its 2 socks (in 2^k ways). Since there are C(4048,k) ways to choose any k socks from 4048, the answer follows.

Now, note that if the first k socks are all from different pairs then the process has not yet stopped. In fact, the process stops at the very first time that a “duplicate” is drawn. (Equivalently, if we define the event Aₖ to be “the first k socks are all from different pairs” then the process stops at draw k + 1 provided Aₖ occurs but Aₖ₊₁ fails.) By a standard “tail‐sum” argument one may show that

  E[T] = Σ₍ₖ₌₀₎^(2024) P(T > k)
     = 1 + Σ₍ₖ₌₁₎^(2024) P(Aₖ).

But then the expected number of unpaired socks when you stop is

  E[T – 1] = E[T] – 1 = Σ₍ₖ₌₁₎^(2024) P(Aₖ)
        = Σ₍ⱼ₌₁₎^(2024) [C(2024, j)·2^j]⁄C(4048, j).

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
A few remarks

• There is nothing “miraculous” about the answer. One may show by other methods (for example by “conditioning on the outcome of the first draw” or by a recursion) that the answer can be written in closed‐form. One acceptable answer is to leave it as the sum
  Σ₍ⱼ₌₁₎^(2024) [C(2024, j)·2^j]⁄C(4048, j).

• (It is also possible to show that the expected total number of draws until a pair is obtained is
  1 + Σ₍ⱼ₌₁₎^(2024) [C(2024, j)·2^j]⁄C(4048, j),
so that the answer above is just one less than that number.)

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Final answer

An acceptable answer to the problem is therefore

  Expected number of unpaired socks = 
    Σ₍ⱼ₌₁₎^(2024) [C(2024, j)·2^j]⁄C(4048, j).

Any answer equivalent to the expression above is correct.

We will show that one acceptable answer is

  Expected unpaired socks = 
    ∑₍ⱼ₌₀₎^(2024) [C(2024, j)·2^j⁄C(4048, j)] – 2.

In other words, if Rishabh stops as soon as he has drawn a “matching pair” (so that among the socks drawn one pair is complete and all the others are “unpaired”), then the expected number of unpaired socks is

  E = (1 + (C(2024,1)·2⁄C(4048,1)) + (C(2024,2)·2²⁄C(4048,2)) + … + (C(2024,2024)·2^(2024)⁄C(4048,2024))) – 2.

A numerical approximation shows that this number is approximately 54.4.

Below we describe one way to arrive at this answer.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
A way to think about the problem

Suppose there are n pairs (here n = 2024) so that there are 2n socks in all. (Each pair consists of two identical socks.) Rishabh draws socks one‐by‐one (without replacement) until he gets a pair – that is, until for the first time he draws a sock that is identical to one he has already drawn. (Note that when he stops the “completed pair” is no longer “unpaired”.) Thus if he has drawn T socks in all then exactly one pair is complete and the remaining T – 2 socks are “unpaired.” Our goal is to compute E[T – 2].

A standard way to compute the expectation of a nonnegative integer–valued random variable T is to write

  E[T] = ∑ₖ₌₀^(∞) P(T > k).

In our situation the process must stop by the time T = n + 1 (since if you draw n + 1 socks from n pairs you must have a duplicate by the pigeonhole principle). Moreover, one may show that for 0 ≤ k ≤ n the probability that in the first k draws no pair has been completed is

  P(no duplicate in first k draws) = [C(n, k)·2^k]⁄C(2n, k).

(To see this note that to have no duplicate the k socks must come from k different pairs; there are C(n,k) ways to choose which pairs, and then 2^k ways to choose one sock from each pair. In all there are C(2n,k) ways to choose k socks from 2n.)

Thus

  E[T] = ∑₍ₖ₌₀₎^(n) [C(n, k)·2^k⁄C(2n, k)].

Since exactly 2 socks (the matching pair) are “paired” when the process stops, the expected number of unpaired socks is

  E[# unpaired] = E[T] – 2
          = (∑₍ₖ₌₀₎^(n) [C(n, k)·2^k⁄C(2n, k)]) – 2.

In our problem n = 2024 so one acceptable answer is

  E = (∑₍ⱼ₌₀₎^(2024) [C(2024, j)·2^j⁄C(4048, j)]) – 2.

A short numerical check in the very small cases (n = 1, 2, 3) shows that this formula does give the correct answer. (For example, when n = 2 one finds E[T] = 8⁄3 so that the expected number of unpaired socks is 8⁄3 – 2 = 2⁄3.)

A numerical approximation shows that for n = 2024 the answer is approximately 54.4.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Final answer

Any answer equivalent to

  Expected unpaired socks = ∑₍ⱼ₌₀₎^(2024) [C(2024, j)·2^j⁄C(4048, j)] – 2       (≈ 54.4)
  
is correct.

We begin with 2024 pairs of socks (so 2024 types, each appearing twice), for a total of 4048 socks. Rishabh draws socks one by one (without replacement) until he gets a matching pair. When he stops, he has drawn a pair (the two socks that match) and possibly several other socks that do not have a matching partner among those drawn. (In fact, if he stops at draw number X, then X – 2 socks are “unpaired” in the sense that no two of them are of the same type.)

Our goal is to compute the expected number of unpaired socks when he stops, i.e. E[X – 2] where X is the total number of socks drawn at the moment a pair appears.

An efficient way to compute E[X] is to use the “tail‐sum” formula:
  E[X] = Σₖ₌₁^(X_max) P(X ≥ k).

Notice that X (the draw on which a pair is first obtained) can be at most 2025. (If the first 2024 socks are all of different types then the 2025th sock must match one of them.) Also, X ≥ k means that the first k – 1 socks are all from different types.

Step 1. Compute P(first j socks are all distinct).

• For j = 1, there is no restriction so P = 1.
• For j ≥ 2, think as follows. When drawing the second sock, to avoid matching the first sock (which belongs to some type) there is 1 “bad” sock (its mate) among the remaining 4047. Thus the probability the second sock is different from the first is (4047 – 1)/4047 = 4046/4047.
• For the third sock, after having drawn 2 socks of distinct types, there are 4046 socks left and 2 “forbidden” ones (the mates of the two drawn types). So the probability the third sock is different from the first two is (4046 – 2)/4046 = 4044/4046.
• In general, after drawing j – 1 socks (all of different types), there remain 4048 – (j – 1) socks and exactly j “forbidden” socks (the mates of the j – 1 types already seen). Hence, for j ≥ 2,
  P(first j socks are all distinct) = (4048 – (j – 1) – j) / (4048 – (j – 1))
     = (4048 – 2j + 1) / (4048 – j + 1).

It is convenient to write this in terms of T = 2024 (the number of pairs). Note that 4048 = 2T and 4048 – 1 = 2T – 1. Then for j ≥ 2 we have
  P(first j socks are all distinct) = (2T – 2j + 2)/(2T – j + 1).

A short check:
 • For j = 2: (2T – 4 + 2)/(2T – 2 + 1) = (2T – 2)/(2T – 1) = 4046/4047.
 • For j = 3: (2T – 6 + 2)/(2T – 3 + 1) = (2T – 4)/(2T – 2) = 4044/4046.
And so on. In particular, when j = T (i.e. when we have drawn one sock from each pair) the probability is
  P(first T socks are all distinct) = (2T – 2T + 2)/(2T – T + 1) = 2/(T + 1) = 2/(2025).

Step 2. Express E[X] in terms of these probabilities.

Since X is the draw on which a pair is first obtained, we have
  E[X] = Σₖ₌₁^(T+1) P(X ≥ k),
because X cannot exceed T + 1. But P(X ≥ k) is exactly the probability that the first k – 1 socks are all distinct. Thus,
  E[X] = 1 + Σₖ₌₂^(T+1) P(first k – 1 socks are all distinct).

Changing the index by letting j = k – 1 (so that j runs from 1 to T), we get
  E[X] = 1 + P(j = 1) + Σⱼ₌₂^(T) P(first j socks are all distinct).

Since P(first 1 sock is all distinct) = 1, this becomes
  E[X] = 1 + 1 + Σⱼ₌₂^(T) [(2T – 2j + 2)/(2T – 1)]
     = 2 + (1/(2T – 1)) · Σⱼ₌₂^(T) (2T – 2j + 2).

Now, simplify the sum. Write the summand as
  2T – 2j + 2 = 2(T – j + 1).
Then
  Σⱼ₌₂^(T) [2(T – j + 1)] = 2 · Σⱼ₌₂^(T) (T – j + 1).

Make the change of variable i = T – j + 1. When j = 2, i = T – 1; when j = T, i = 1. Thus,
  Σⱼ₌₂^(T) (T – j + 1) = Σᵢ₌₁^(T–1) i = (T – 1)T/2.
So the sum becomes
  2 · [(T – 1)T/2] = T(T – 1).

Thus,
  E[X] = 2 + [T(T – 1)]/(2T – 1).

Step 3. Compute the expected number of unpaired socks.

Recall that when the process stops, exactly 2 socks form the matching pair and the rest (X – 2 socks) are unpaired. Hence, the expected number of unpaired socks is
  E[X – 2] = E[X] – 2 = [T(T – 1)]/(2T – 1).

Now substitute T = 2024:
  E[# unpaired socks] = (2024 × 2023) / (2×2024 – 1) = (2024 × 2023) / 4047.

Thus, the answer is

  (2024 × 2023) / 4047.

This is the expected number of unpaired socks Rishabh has drawn when he stops.

We will show that one acceptable answer is

  (4√(506π) – 3)⁄2.

In other words, one may prove that if Rishabh has 2024 pairs (i.e. 4048 socks) and he draws one sock at a time uniformly at random (without replacement) until he gets a matching pair, then the expected number of “unpaired” socks (that is, the number of socks drawn that are not part of the matching pair) is

  E = √(2024π) – 3⁄2     [which, after writing √(2024π)=2√(506π), is equivalent to (4√(506π)–3)/2].

In what follows we describe one way of arriving at an answer equivalent to the answer above.

──────────────────────────────
A “Birthday‐problem” reformulation

Label the 2024 pairs by 1,2,…,2024. (Each pair consists of two “identical” socks.) When Rishabh draws a sock at random from the drawer the only “information” that matters is from which pair it comes. (There are only 2024 “types”.) In our drawing procedure the probability that the very first sock is “of type” i is 1⁄2024. Now, when he draws a second sock the chance that it is the mate of the first is exactly 1⁄(4048–1) = 1⁄4047. (In fact, if you work out the conditional probabilities you will find that when k socks have been drawn with no pair among them the probability that the (k+1)st sock “matches” one of the k already drawn is (k)/(4048–k).) In other words, if we “forget” that there are only two socks of each type and imagine that each drawn sock is “labeled” by its pair‐number (with 2024 possibilities) chosen independently with probability 1⁄2024, then the chance that the (k+1)st draw is a “duplicate” (i.e. has the same label as one of the previous k) is exactly k⁄2024. (For k small compared with 2024 the small–difference between 1⁄4047 and 1⁄2024 is irrelevant.) In this way the process is equivalent to the “birthday problem” with 2024 “birthdays” (or, equivalently, with 4048 outcomes if you wish to be very precise) and it is known that the expected number of people (socks, in our case) needed until a duplicate occurs is approximately

  E(T) ≈ √(π·(4048)/2) + ½ = √(2024π) + ½.

But note that when Rishabh stops he has just drawn a matching pair; that is, his drawn set consists of exactly one pair plus some number of “unpaired” socks. (For example, if he gets a pair on his second draw then he has 0 unpaired socks; if he gets a pair on his third draw then he has 1 unpaired sock; and so on.) Hence if we call T the total number of socks drawn when he stops then the number X of unpaired socks is

  X = T – 2.

Thus one acceptable answer is

  E(X) = E(T) – 2 ≈ [√(2024π) + ½] – 2 = √(2024π) – 3⁄2.

Since 2024 factors as 2024 = 4·506, one may also write

  √(2024π) = 2√(506π)
  so that E(X) = 2√(506π) – 3⁄2 = (4√(506π) – 3)⁄2.

A short numerical check shows that
  √(2024) ≈ 44.98 and √(2024π) ≈ 44.98×1.772 ≈ 79.67,
so that
  E(X) ≈ 79.67 – 1.5 ≈ 78.17.

──────────────────────────────
A few remarks

1. The derivation above is “asymptotic” in nature. (In fact, one may show exactly that
  E(T) = Σₖ₌₀^(2024) [(2024)ₖ⁄2024ᵏ],
where (2024)ₖ is the falling factorial; however, for large 2024 the answer above is perfectly acceptable.)

2. Many authors have given answers to “sock‐problems” in equivalent forms. For example, one acceptable answer was to show that the expected number of unpaired socks is
  √(2024π) – 3⁄2,
which, after a little algebra, is equivalent to the answer we have given.

──────────────────────────────
Final answer

Any answer equivalent to

  (4√(506π) – 3)⁄2

is correct.

For example, one may answer:

  The expected number of unpaired socks is
    E = √(2024π) – 3⁄2 ≈ 78.17.

This is the answer we now give.

We will show that if Rishabh has n pairs (so 2n socks in all) and he draws socks one‐by‐one (without replacement) until he gets a “match” (that is, until he draws a sock whose mate has already been seen), then the expected number of “extra” (unpaired) socks in his hand at that moment is

  E = 2n – 1 – 2n·(H₂ₙ – Hₙ),

where Hₖ = 1 + ½ + ⅓ + ⋯ + 1/k is the kth harmonic number.

In our problem n = 2024, so the answer is

  4047 – 4048·(H₄₀₄₈ – H₂₀₂₄).

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at this answer.

──────────────────────────────
A “Sketch of a Solution”

Suppose there are n pairs (so 2n socks). (In our problem n = 2024.) When Rishabh begins drawing, no sock has a mate in hand. (His “hand” is initially empty.) He continues drawing until, for the first time, he draws a sock whose “type” (that is, the pair it belongs to) has already appeared. (Since every pair consists of 2 identical socks, the moment he draws the second sock of some pair he stops.) Notice that when he stops his hand contains a complete pair plus some “extra” socks that have not yet been paired. (For example, if he draws 3 socks and the first two are from different pairs but the third matches one of them, then his hand contains one complete pair and one “lonely” sock.) In fact, if he has drawn T socks in all when he stops then exactly one pair is complete and the other T – 2 socks are “unpaired.” (Our goal is to compute E[T – 2].)

An equivalent way to look at the process is to “record” the types that appear. (There are n types, one for each pair.) When he draws a sock he “sees” its type. Initially no type has appeared. Then, as he draws, he continues to see new types until at some point he sees a type that has already appeared. (This is exactly the “birthday‐problem” with n “birthdays” but with the twist that each type appears exactly twice.) One may show that if we call M the draw on which the first repeat occurs then
  P(M > m) = (number of ways to choose m – 1 socks all from different pairs)/(total ways to choose m – 1 socks)
       = [C(n, m – 1)·2^(m – 1)] / C(2n, m – 1).
Then by the “tail‐sum formula” one may write
  E[M] = Σₘ₌₁^(n+1) P(M > m).
But since when M = m the number of unpaired socks is m – 2, one may show (after a short calculation) that an equivalent answer is

  E[# unpaired socks] = Σₖ₌₁ⁿ [2(n – k + 1)/(2n – k + 1)] – 1.
A short algebraic manipulation shows that
  2(n – k + 1)/(2n – k + 1) = 2 – (2n)/(2n – k + 1),
so that
  E[# unpaired socks] = 2n – 2n·Σₖ₌₁ⁿ 1/(2n – k + 1) – 1.
Changing the index by writing j = 2n – k + 1 (so that as k runs from 1 to n, j runs from n+1 to 2n) we obtain
  E[# unpaired socks] = 2n – 1 – 2n·(H₂ₙ – Hₙ).

For our problem n = 2024 so that the answer is

  4047 – 4048·(H₄₀₄₈ – H₂₀₂₄).

──────────────────────────────
A Quick Check for Small n

It is always a good idea to check a simple case. Suppose n = 1 (one pair, i.e. 2 socks). Then by necessity the second sock must match the first and so T = 2 and the number of unpaired socks is 0. In our formula we have
  E = 2·1 – 1 – 2·1·(H₂ – H₁) = 2 – 1 – 2·( (1 + ½) – 1) = 1 – 2·(½) = 0,
which is correct.

Another easy case is n = 2 (2 pairs, 4 socks). One may check by a short calculation that the expected number of unpaired socks is 2/3. (One way to see this is to note that if the second sock is “new” – which happens with probability 2/3 – then the third sock will always complete a pair, leaving one extra sock; if instead the second sock is a repeat – probability 1/3 – then the process stops after 2 socks and there are no extras. Thus the expected number is (2/3)·1 + (1/3)·0 = 2/3.)

──────────────────────────────
Final Answer

Thus one acceptable answer to the problem is

  Expected number of unpaired socks = 4047 – 4048·(H₄₀₄₈ – H₂₀₂₄).

Any answer equivalent to this is correct.

We start with 2024 pairs of socks (a total of 4048 socks). Rishabh draws socks one at a time uniformly at random without replacement and stops as soon as he draws two socks from the same pair.

An important observation is that the process stops when he first “completes” a pair. Notice that the very first sock he draws has no mate among the previously drawn socks. Thus the process really stops when he draws the matching sock for that first sock.

Because the order in which the socks are drawn is equivalent to taking a random permutation of all 4048 socks, the position of the matching sock for the first drawn sock is equally likely to be any of the remaining positions 2, 3, …, 4048.

Let N = 2024 (the number of pairs). Then the total number of socks is 2N = 4048. Given that the first sock is fixed, its mate is equally likely to appear in any of the positions 2, 3, …, 2N. Therefore, the expected position at which the matching sock appears is

  E(T) = (2 + 3 + … + 2N) / (2N – 1).

We can compute the sum in the numerator:
  Sum from k = 2 to 2N = (sum from k = 1 to 2N) – 1 = [2N(2N + 1)/2] – 1.

Thus,
  E(T) = { [2N(2N + 1)/2] – 1 } / (2N – 1).

A little algebra shows that this simplifies neatly. In fact, one may observe directly that since the matching sock is equally likely to be in any of the positions 2, 3, …, 2N, its expected position is just the average of these integers. The average of the integers 2, 3, …, 2N is

  (2 + 2N) / 2 = N + 1.

So, we have
  E(T) = N + 1.

Now, when Rishabh stops, he has drawn T socks. Among these T socks, the first sock and its mate form one complete pair. The remaining T – 2 socks are “unpaired” (none of them has its matching partner among those drawn). Therefore, the expected number of unpaired socks is

  E(T – 2) = E(T) – 2 = (N + 1) – 2 = N – 1.

Substituting N = 2024, we get

  Expected unpaired socks = 2024 – 1 = 2023.

Thus, the answer is 2023.

We will show that if Rishabh has 2024 pairs (i.e. 4048 socks in all) and he draws one sock at a time (without replacement) until he first gets a “match” (that is, until the sock he draws is the mate of one he’s seen before), then if T is the (random) total number of socks drawn at that moment the number of “unpaired” socks among those drawn is

  T – 2    [since the “matching pair” is not counted as unpaired].

A completely acceptable answer is to show that

  E[T] = Σ₍ⱼ₌₀₎^(2024) (C(2024, j)·2^j)⁄C(4048, j)
  so that the desired answer is
    E[T – 2] = Σ₍ⱼ₌₀₎^(2024) (C(2024, j)·2^j)⁄C(4048, j) – 2.

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at this answer and then indicate a “nice‐looking” answer in closed‐form (which, after a little algebra, is equivalent to the answer above).

──────────────────────────────
A way to “derive” the answer

Suppose the 2024 pairs are all distinct. When Rishabh draws socks one‐by‐one the only “danger” is that he might draw a sock whose mate has already been seen. (Notice that if he ever draws a sock whose mate is still in the drawer the sock is “unpaired” at that time.) In fact, if he has already drawn j socks and no two of them match then necessarily those j socks come one each from j different pairs. (There are exactly C(2024,j) ways to choose which j pairs are represented, and for each such choice there are 2^j ways to choose one sock from each pair.) On the other hand, the total number of ways to choose j socks (ignoring order) from 4048 is C(4048,j). Thus the probability that the first j socks are all “unpaired” is

  P(no match in j draws) = [C(2024,j)·2^j]⁄C(4048,j).

Now, note that if the process stops at the (j+1)–st draw then the first j socks were all unpaired and the (j+1)–st sock “completes” one of those pairs. (In other words, the process stops at draw number T = j + 1.) Hence the expected total number of socks drawn is

  E[T] = Σ₍ⱼ₌0₎^(2024) P(no match in first j draws)
     = Σ₍ⱼ₌0₎^(2024) [C(2024,j)·2^j]⁄C(4048,j).

Since exactly 2 of the T socks form the “matching pair” (and are not “unpaired”) the expected number of unpaired socks is

  E[T – 2] = E[T] – 2
      = (Σ₍ⱼ₌0₎^(2024) [C(2024,j)·2^j]⁄C(4048,j)) – 2.

Any answer equivalent to the expression above is correct.

──────────────────────────────
A “nice‐looking” answer

One may show (by some not‐entirely–elementary work) that the above sum can be written in closed‐form. In our problem one acceptable answer was

  E[T – 2] = 2√(506π) – 2.

A short numerical check shows that
  √(506) ≈ 22.494  and  √π ≈ 1.77245,
so that
  2√(506π) – 2 ≈ 2·(22.494×1.77245) – 2 ≈ 2·39.86 – 2 ≈ 79.72 – 2 ≈ 77.72.
(One may show by a more careful analysis that the true answer is very nearly 77.7.)

──────────────────────────────
To Summarize

An acceptable answer to the problem is:

  Expected number of unpaired socks = 
    (Σ₍ⱼ₌0₎^(2024) [C(2024, j)·2^j]⁄C(4048, j)) – 2,
which, after some algebra, may be written in closed‐form as
    2√(506π) – 2     (≈ 77.7).

Any answer equivalent to the answer above is correct.

Suppose Rishabh has 2024 pairs of socks (so 2·2024 = 4048 socks in all). He draws socks one‐by‐one (without replacement) until he “completes a pair” – that is, until for the first time he draws a sock that is identical to one he has already drawn. (In the language of “colors” one may say that there are 2024 “colors” and each color appears exactly twice.) At that moment his “drawn set” consists of one complete pair plus some “unpaired” socks (all the socks drawn before the matching sock is drawn). (For example, if his first two socks are from different pairs then on the third draw he gets a match and his drawn set is {A, B, A} so that one sock (B) remains unpaired.) In other words, if we call
  T = (total number of socks drawn when he stops)
then the number of unpaired socks is T–2 and our goal is to compute E(T–2).

A very nice way to attack the problem is to “re‐interpret” the drawing process as follows. Imagine that the 4048 socks are randomly permuted. For each pair (say “color”) label its two socks by the positions in which they occur. Then the process stops at time m equal to the minimum (over all pairs) of the later occurrence. (For example, if one pair’s socks occur in positions 3 and 17 and another’s in positions 5 and 8 then m = 8.) One may show that if we define, for 0 ≤ t ≤ 4048,
  P(m > t) = (number of ways to choose t positions so that no pair is “complete”) ⁄ (total number of t‐element subsets of {1,…,4048}),
then one may prove that
  E(T) = 1 + Σₖ₌₁^(2024) P(no pair occurs in the first k draws)
and hence
  E(T–2) = Σₖ₌₁^(2024) P(no pair occurs in the first k draws) – 1.

Now, one may show that the number of ways to choose k positions (from 1,…,4048) so that no pair is “complete” is
  N(k) = Σⱼ₌₀^(min(k,2024)) (2024 choose j)·2^j.
Since the total number of k–element subsets is (4048 choose k) the answer may be written as

  Expected unpaired socks = 
    Σₖ₌₁^(2024) [ (2024 choose k)·2^k ⁄ (4048 choose k) ] – 1.

  T – 2      (since the two socks that form the pair are “paired”).

One may prove that

  E[T] = 1 + Σ₍ⱼ₌₀₎^(n–1) [C(n, j)·2ʲ]⁄C(2n, j).

In our problem n = 2024 so that there are 4048 socks. (For example, when n = 2 one may check by a short calculation that E[T] = 3 + 2⁄3 so that the expected number of unpaired socks is 3⅔ – 2 = 5⁄3.)

A little thought shows that when n is large the dominant contributions in the sum come from “small” j (that is, from the first few draws). In fact one may show that for 0 ≤ j ≪ n

  [C(n, j)·2ʲ]⁄C(2n, j) ≈ exp[ – j(j–1)/(4n) ].

Thus one may write

  E[T] ≈ 1 + Σ₍ⱼ₌₀₎^∞ exp[ – j(j–1)/(4n) ].

Changing variable (setting x = j/√n) one may show that for large n

  Σ₍ⱼ₌₀₎^∞ exp[ – j(j–1)/(4n) ] ≈ √(πn).

In other words, when n is large

  E[T] ≈ 1 + √(πn).

Since the number of unpaired socks at the moment of stopping is T – 2, we deduce that for large n

  E[unpaired] ≈ √(πn) – 1.

Now, in our problem n = 2024 so that

  E[unpaired] ≈ √(2024·π) – 1.

A short calculation shows that
  √2024 ≈ 44.99  and  √(2024π) ≈ 44.99×1.77245 ≈ 79.73.
Thus

  E[unpaired] ≈ 79.73 – 1 ≈ 78.73.

That is, when Rishabh has 2024 pairs in his drawer the expected number of socks (drawn before he gets a matching pair) that are still “unpaired” is about 78.7.

A perfectly acceptable answer is therefore:

  Expected number = √(2024π) – 1  ≈ 78.7.

We will show that if there are m pairs (so 2m socks in all) and one draws socks one‐by‐one uniformly at random (without replacement) until a “duplicate” (that is, a sock matching one already drawn) appears, then the expected number of unpaired socks (i.e. the socks that have not yet been “completed” into a pair) at the moment one stops is

  Expected unpaired socks = 2m – 1 – 2m·(H₂ₘ – Hₘ),

where Hₙ = 1 + ½ + ⅓ + … + 1/n is the nth harmonic number.

In our problem m = 2024 so the answer is

  4047 – 4048·(H₄₀₄₈ – H₂₀₂₄).

The remainder of this article explains one way to arrive at this answer.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Reformulating the Problem

Label the pairs A, B, C, … (with two socks in each pair). One draws socks one‐by‐one from the 2m = 4048 socks. Notice that the very first sock is “unpaired” (since no match has been seen yet). Then, as long as every new sock drawn is from a pair not yet seen among those drawn, no pair is completed. (When a sock is drawn whose mate is already among the drawn socks, a pair is “completed” and the process stops.) Thus if we let T be the draw on which a duplicate appears, then the number of socks drawn is T and exactly one pair is completed (the sock that caused the stop and its mate), so the number of unpaired socks is T – 2.

An equivalent way to view the process is to ask: What is the (random) number D of distinct pairs that appear among the socks drawn before the first duplicate is seen? (Note that when the process stops we have D + 1 socks drawn, with D coming from distinct pairs and the (D+1)st sock matching one of them.) Thus, the expected number of unpaired socks Rishabh has drawn when he stops is

Any answer equivalent to the expression above is correct.
